paragraphs: “To begin with, where did this suspicion come from?” (Ippolit Kirillovitch began.) “The first person to cry out that Smerdyakov had committed the murder was the prisoner himself, at the moment of his arrest. Yet from that day to this he has not offered a single fact to support the charge, nor even the faintest hint of one. Only three people back it up: the prisoner’s two brothers and Madame Svyetlov. The elder brother voiced his suspicions only today, when he was undoubtedly in the grip of brain fever. We know, though, that for the last two months he fully shared our conviction of his brother’s guilt and made no attempt to argue against it. But more of that later. The younger brother has admitted that he has not the slightest fact to support his notion of Smerdyakov’s guilt. He was led to it only by the prisoner’s own words and the look on his face. Yes, that astounding piece of evidence he has offered twice today. Madame Svyetlov was more astounding still. ‘What the prisoner tells you, you must believe; he is not a man to tell a lie.’ That is all the evidence these three witnesses have produced against Smerdyakov, and all three are deeply concerned in the prisoner’s fate. And yet the theory of Smerdyakov’s guilt has been noised about, and is still maintained. Is that credible? Is it even conceivable?”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it necessary to describe the character of Smerdyakov, “who had ended his life in a fit of insanity.” He portrayed him as a man of weak mind with a smattering of education. Philosophical ideas beyond his level had thrown him off balance, as had certain modern theories of duty. He had learned those theories in practice from the reckless life of his master, who was perhaps also his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch. In theory he had learned them from various strange philosophical conversations with his master’s elder son, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who readily indulged in this pastime, probably out of boredom or to amuse himself at the valet’s expense. “He spoke to me himself about his state of mind during his last few days in his father’s house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained. “But others have also borne witness to it: the prisoner himself, his brother, and the servant Grigory. That is, everyone who knew him well.

“Moreover, Smerdyakov’s health was shaken by his epileptic attacks, and he had not the courage of a chicken. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the prisoner himself has told us, before he realized how damaging that statement was to himself. ‘He is an epileptic chicken,’ he said of him, in his own characteristic language. The prisoner chose him as his confidant (we have his own word for it) and frightened him until he finally agreed to act as a spy for him. In that role he betrayed his master. He told the prisoner that the envelope with the notes existed, and he told him the signals by which he could get into the house. And how could he have refused to tell him? ‘He would have killed me, I could see that he would have killed me,’ he said at the inquiry. He was trembling and shaking even in front of us, though his tormentor had by then been arrested and could do him no harm. ‘He suspected me every minute. In fear and trembling I hurried to tell him every secret to calm him, so that he would see I had not deceived him and let me off alive.’ Those are his own words. I wrote them down, and I remember them. ‘When he began shouting at me, I would fall on my knees.’

“He was naturally very honest, and he had enjoyed his master’s complete confidence ever since he returned some money his master had lost. So we may suppose that the poor fellow suffered pangs of remorse at having deceived a master he loved as his benefactor. People severely afflicted with epilepsy are, so the most skillful doctors tell us, always prone to continual, morbid self-reproach. They worry over their ‘wickedness.’ They are tormented by their consciences, often entirely without cause. They exaggerate, and often invent, all sorts of faults and crimes. And here we have a man of that type, who had really been driven to wrongdoing by terror and intimidation.

“Besides, he had a strong foreboding that something terrible would come of the situation developing before his eyes. Ivan Fyodorovitch was about to leave for Moscow, just before the catastrophe. Smerdyakov begged him to stay, but was too timid to say plainly what he feared. He only dropped hints, and nobody understood them.

“Note that he looked on Ivan Fyodorovitch as a protector. While Ivan was in the house, he felt, no harm could happen. Remember the phrase in Dmitri Karamazov’s drunken letter: ‘I shall kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away.’ So everyone took Ivan Fyodorovitch’s presence as a guarantee of peace and order in the house.

“But he left, and within an hour Smerdyakov, after his young master’s departure, was struck by an epileptic fit. That is perfectly understandable. I must mention here that Smerdyakov, weighed down by terror and a kind of despair, had sensed over those last few days that one of the fits he had suffered before at moments of strain might be coming on again. The day and hour of such an attack cannot, of course, be foreseen, but every epileptic can feel beforehand that one is likely. So the doctors tell us. And so, the moment Ivan Fyodorovitch had driven out of the yard, Smerdyakov, low-spirited at being left alone and unprotected, went to the cellar. Going down the stairs he asked himself whether a fit would come, and what if it came on him right then. And that very dread, that very asking, brought on the spasm in his throat that always comes before such attacks, and he fell unconscious into the cellar. And in this perfectly natural event people try to find grounds for suspicion, a hint that he was shamming the attack _on purpose_. But if it was on purpose, the question arises at once: what was his motive? What was he counting on? What was he aiming at? I say nothing about medicine. Science, I am told, may go astray, and the doctors could not tell the counterfeit from the real. That may be so, but answer me one question: what motive had he for such a counterfeit? If he had been plotting the murder, would he have wanted to draw the household’s attention by having a fit just beforehand?

“You see, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the murder there were five people at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s. There was Fyodor Pavlovitch himself (but he did not kill himself, that is evident). Then there was his servant, Grigory, but he was almost killed himself. The third was Grigory’s wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, but it would be simply shameful to imagine her murdering her master. Two people are left: the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Now, if we are to believe the prisoner’s statement that he is not the murderer, then Smerdyakov must have been, for there is no other alternative, and no one else can be found. That is what accounts for the artful, astounding accusation against the unhappy idiot who committed suicide yesterday. Had a shadow of suspicion rested on anyone else, had there been any sixth person, I am convinced that even the prisoner would have been ashamed to accuse Smerdyakov. He would have accused that sixth person, for to charge Smerdyakov with this murder is perfectly absurd.

“Gentlemen, let us lay aside psychology, let us lay aside medicine, let us even lay aside logic. Let us turn only to the facts and see what the facts tell us. If Smerdyakov killed him, how did he do it? Alone, or with the prisoner’s help? Let us consider the first possibility, that he did it alone. If he killed him, it must have been for some purpose, for some advantage to himself. But he had not a shadow of the motives the prisoner had for the murder: hatred, jealousy, and so on. So Smerdyakov could only have murdered him for gain, to take the three thousand roubles he had seen his master put in the envelope. And yet he tells another person, and a person most closely interested, that is, the prisoner, everything about the money and the signals. He tells him where the envelope lay, what was written on it, what it was tied up with, and above all he tells him the signals by which he could enter the house. Did he do this simply to betray himself? Or to invite into the same enterprise a man who would be eager to get that envelope for himself? ‘Yes,’ I shall be told, ‘but he gave it away out of fear.’ But how do you explain this? A man who could conceive such an audacious, savage act, and carry it out, tells facts which no one else in the world knows, and which no one would ever have guessed if he had held his tongue!

“No. However cowardly he might be, if he had plotted such a crime, nothing would have made him tell anyone about the envelope and the signals, for that was as good as betraying himself beforehand. He would have invented something. If he had been forced to give information, he would have told some lie, but he would have kept silent about that. Consider the other course. Suppose he had said nothing about the money, but had committed the murder and taken it. Then nobody in the world could have accused him of murder for robbery, since he alone had seen the money and he alone knew it was in the house. Even if he had been accused of the murder, people could only have supposed some other motive. But no one had noticed any such motive in him beforehand. On the contrary, everyone saw that his master was fond of him and honored him with his confidence. So he would, of course, have been the last to be suspected. People would have suspected first the man who had a motive, a man who had himself declared he had such motives and had made no secret of it. They would, in fact, have suspected the murdered man’s son, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Had Smerdyakov killed and robbed him, and the son been accused of it, that would, of course, have suited Smerdyakov. Yet are we to believe that, though he was plotting the murder, he told that son, Dmitri, about the money, the envelope and the signals? Is that logical? Is that clear?

“Now the day of the murder planned by Smerdyakov comes, and we have him tumbling downstairs in a _feigned_ fit. With what object? First, so that Grigory, who had been meaning to take his medicine, might put it off and stay on guard, seeing that there was no one else to watch the house. Second, I suppose, so that his master, seeing there was no one to guard him and in terror of a visit from his son, might redouble his vigilance and precautions. And most of all, I suppose, so that he, Smerdyakov, disabled by the fit, would be carried out of the kitchen, where he always slept apart from all the rest and could come and go as he liked, and put in Grigory’s room at the other end of the lodge. That was where he was always put, behind a screen three paces from their own bed. This was the old custom, set by his master and the kind-hearted Marfa Ignatyevna, whenever he had a fit. There, lying behind the screen, he would most likely, to keep up the sham, have begun groaning, and so kept them awake all night (as Grigory and his wife testified). And all this, we are to believe, so that he could more conveniently get up and murder his master!
